summary: This paper applies the Markov-ICL framework to Mamba and provides the first connection between selective SSMs and optimal statistical estimators, showing empirically that a single-layer Mamba learns the in-context Laplacian smoothing (add-beta) estimator for all Markov orders, and theoretically that a simplified MambaZero can represent it for first-order chains, plus a 2^k lower bound on hidden dimension for any recurrent model. The core insight that convolution (more than gating/nonlinearity) drives this ability is well-supported by ablations and extends plausibly to non-Markovian and language settings. The contribution is novel and valuable for the SSM-theory community, but the theory covers only first-order chains and a simplified model while the abstract emphasizes 'all Markov orders,' key experimental evidence is largely deferred to appendices, and statistical reporting is uneven.
strengths: First work to connect Mamba/SSMs to a classical Bayes-and-minimax-optimal estimator (Laplacian smoothing), giving the Markov-ICL framework a principled statistical interpretation for SSMs.

Clean constructive proof (Thm 1) for first-order chains that is explicitly aligned with the structures empirically learned by the model (a_t near 1, b^(ij) dot c_t near 0 for i != x_t), making the theory explanatory rather than merely existential.

Non-trivial lower bound (Thm 2) showing any recurrent architecture needs hidden dimension scaling as ~2^k to implement the kth-order Laplacian estimator, usefully contrasting with the linear-in-k transformer result.

Well-designed ablations isolating convolution vs gating vs nonlinearity (Fig 3a) and the window-size/order relationship (Fig 3b), plus a switching-Markov setting that finally activates the selectivity mechanism a_t and a WikiText-103 probe of the convolution insight.

Honest scoping: the authors clearly state Thm 1 is first-order only and that higher orders are empirically 'strongly suggested,' and frame the work as understanding Mamba rather than a Mamba-vs-Transformer horse race.

key_concerns.issue: The abstract, title framing, and contribution bullet claim Mamba learns the optimal estimator 'for all Markov orders,' but Theorem 1 only proves representability for first-order chains on the simplified MambaZero model; higher orders are supported only empirically (Fig 1b, Fig 10 in appendix). The theory-claim gap is not just a wording issue because the central theoretical guarantee does not cover the headline claim.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either extend the construction to kth-order chains (at least for MambaZero with w=k+1, which the proof sketch suggests may be feasible), or explicitly and repeatedly scope the 'all orders' claim as empirical and reserve the theoretical claim for first-order; consider proving a kth-order representability theorem even if the dimension blows up per Thm 2.

key_concerns.issue: Several pieces of evidence central to the main claims appear only as appendix references in the main text (Figs 9, 10, 13 for over-parametrization, larger state spaces/deeper models, and the switching-Markov selectivity demonstration), so a reader of the main body cannot fully evaluate the breadth of support.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Promote at least one figure each for (a) larger state spaces / deeper models and (b) the switching-Markov a_t dynamics into the main text, since these underpin the generality and the selectivity story respectively.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical reporting is inconsistent: Fig 1b reports std over 5 runs, but most other comparisons (Fig 3, Table 1, appendix figures) report point estimates with no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests, making it hard to judge whether the Mamba-vs-Transformer 'sharpness' differences and the 11% vs 2% WikiText-103 gap are statistically real.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add error bars/seeds for all quantitative comparisons and report significance (or at least effect size with variance) for the WikiText-103 perplexity differences and the convolution-ablation losses.

key_concerns.issue: The natural-language evidence for the 'convolution is key' generalization claim rests on a single dataset (WikiText-103) and very small models (~14M params), and the paper itself notes the convolution effect shrinks with depth (Table 5), so the generality of the claim beyond the synthetic regime is under-supported.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either scope the language claim to small-scale models explicitly, or add at least one more dataset / a larger model checkpoint to substantiate that convolution's saliency holds beyond the 14M-parameter regime.

questions_for_authors: Can the Theorem 1 construction be extended to kth-order chains for MambaZero with window w=k+1, and if so what is the resulting hidden dimension (does it match the 2^k lower bound up to constants)?
Is the a_t near 1 regime in Section 4.2.1 a provable consequence of the loss landscape, or purely an empirical observation? Does the construction still hold if a_t deviates slightly from 1?

For the switching-Markov result, how sensitive is the reset behavior (a_t dropping to 0 at switch tokens) to the switch probability p_switch, and does the model still recover the add-beta estimator between switches for small p_switch?

Given Thm 2's 2^k lower bound for recurrent models vs the linear-in-k transformer bound you cite, how do you reconcile this with the empirical observation that 1-layer Mamba tracks the optimal estimator sharply even at order 4 (Fig 1b) -- is the constant in the bound small, or is the regime below the bound's threshold?
calibration_check: Claims are mostly well-scoped and limitations (first-order-only theory, no learning-dynamics analysis) are stated openly, but the abstract's 'for all Markov orders' phrasing modestly outruns the theoretical guarantee, which is first-order only.

significance.justification: First principled link between Mamba and optimal estimators is a meaningful advance for SSM theory that the community will cite and build on, though the synthetic Markov sandbox limits broader impact.

novelty.justification: First application of the Markov-ICL framework to Mamba/SSMs and the first connection to Laplacian smoothing; the convolution-as-key insight is genuinely new.

rigor.justification: Constructive proof and lower bound are sound, but the theory covers only first-order chains on a simplified model while headline claims extend further, leaving a theory-practice gap.

statistical_soundness.justification: Only Fig 1b reports variance (5 runs); most other results and Table 1 are point estimates with no error bars or significance tests, so key improvements are not shown to be statistically real.

calibration_honesty.justification: Limitations are stated openly and claims are largely scoped to evidence, with only mild overreach in the abstract's 'all Markov orders' framing relative to the first-order theorem.

clarity.justification: Generally readable with a well-explained construction, but the architecture section is hard to parse and many central results are pushed to appendices, fragmenting the argument.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard conference structure is followed with reasonable length, though over-reliance on appendix figures weakens the main-body narrative.

reproducibility.justification: Data generation and the constructive proof are described in enough detail to reproduce, but most hyperparameters and training details live in appendices not shown here.

related_work.justification: Prior work on SSMs, transformer ICL, and the Markov-ICL framework is fairly represented and the contribution is clearly delineated, including honest mention of conflicting Mamba-vs-Transformer evidence.

figure_quality.justification: Captions are informative and each display item supports a specific claim, but too few figures sit in the main body to let a reader verify breadth without the appendix.

breadth_generality.justification: Orders 1-4, binary and larger state spaces, switching-Markov, and one language dataset are covered, but theory is first-order only and language evidence is small-scale, so claimed generality is moderately under-supported.

overall_recommendation.justification: A sound, novel, and useful contribution that clears the borderline-accept bar; fixable issues in scoping, main-text evidence, and statistical reporting keep it just below a clear accept.
